paper.title_en: The Changing Meaning of One-Loop Exactness in $\mathcal{N}=2$ Supersymmetric Yang--Mills Theory
paper.abstract_en:
One of the striking achievements of supersymmetric field theory was to
recast difficult perturbative statements in increasingly compact
structures governed by symmetry, analyticity, holomorphy, and geometry.
In four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric Yang--Mills theory, the phrase
``one-loop exact'' records this development especially clearly.  This
survey reconstructs the quantum-field-theoretic statements compressed
into that phrase.  Early multiloop calculations and supergraph/background-field methods established an ultraviolet theorem about higher-loop
gauge-coupling counterterms.  Work on $\mathcal{N}=2$ quantization, dimensional
reduction, and invariant regulators then exposed the prescriptions needed
to realize that theorem in perturbation theory.  Anomaly and holomorphy
arguments reorganized the protected information in terms of distinguished
Wilsonian couplings, while Seiberg's 1988 formulation connected it to
non-perturbative physics.  In Seiberg--Witten theory the same slogan came
to describe the perturbative truncation of the Coulomb-branch
prepotential, whose exact form nevertheless contains instanton
corrections.  We distinguish holomorphic Wilsonian, canonically normalized,
1PI, and Coulomb-branch couplings and show explicitly why finite scheme
changes delimit all-orders beta-function statements.  The pre-Seiberg
origin of the non-renormalization theorem is well preserved in specialist
literature; priority revision is therefore not the main claim.  Rather,
the history is treated as a sequence of translations from ultraviolet
renormalization to holomorphic low-energy geometry.  Recovering the QFT
vocabulary of counterterms, regulators, Ward identities, prescriptions,
and effective actions identifies the physical content that the later,
more economical language encodes.
